items.abstract: Abstract This paper explores sustainability mindsets, which have received increasing attention in the corporate sustainability management literature. Sustainability mindsets often appear as peripheral but necessary for successful corporate sustainability management. However, despite these references in the academic literature, the discussion lacks theoretical foundation. To analyze and advance the concept of both individual and organizational sustainability mindsets, the paper draws on Gollwitzer’s mindset theory of action phases as a theoretical perspective, in particular on goal setting and striving, implementation intentions as well as action control. The paper identifies the need to link organizational sustainability goals to individual goals of employees. It shows that implementation intentions (also called if–then plans) can be beneficial in corporate sustainability management but an important part is to establish a goal hierarchy when multiple goals exist, which is often the case in a multi-faceted sustainability strategy. A possible solution is to prioritize different goals for different teams based on their strengths. Furthermore, integrating sustainability into organizational and individual routines and creating a level of automaticity is an important element that corporate sustainability management can benefit from. A normative, processual framework is proposed, inspired by Gollwitzer’s mindset theory of action phases and what corporate sustainability management can learn from it. The conceptual paper contributes to the academic literature by attempting a definition of individual sustainability mindsets as well as an organizational sustainability mindset and how corporate sustainability management can support and subsequently benefit from the development of these mindsets.
items.title: Sustainability Mindsets in Corporate Sustainability Management: A Theoretical Exploration from the Mindset Theory of Action Phases

items.abstract: Abstract In this paper, we initiate the project of articulating an existentialist constitutivist ethical theory, specifically a Sartrean one. Standardly, constitutivism argues that every action is constituted by at least one fundamental normative claim—call this the Constitutivist Criterion. We begin with the formulation of a problem (the Problem of Necessity) that faces every constitutivist ethical theory, namely, the problem of justifying the necessary character of its Constitutivist Criterion. We then identify a problem (the Criterion Problem) which is specific for an existentialist, particularly Sartrean constitutivist theory, namely its compatibility with a universal ethical criterion. We show that Sartrean existentialist constitutivism can answer the Criterion Problem and can offer a better solution to the Problem of Necessity than those few ethical theories that can also answer it. We consider a potential objection to Sartrean existentialist constitutivism starting from Sartre’s conception of radical freedom, often regarded as leading to implausible implications. We answer this objection, present the argument in support of the Sartrean constitutivist criterion (authenticity) and conclude by identifying some of the limitations of our argument and some lines of inquiry for future work.
items.title: Existentialist Constitutivism: Sartrean Authenticity and Kantian Synthesis

items.abstract: Over the past two decades, “personal identity change” has become a central term in the neuroethics literature for articulating the ethical risks associated with deep brain stimulation (DBS). Yet its referential boundaries, conditions of conceptual admissibility, and proper scope of application remain insufficiently clarified. This article argues that the term is subject to systematic conceptual confusion in neuroethics because it is routinely expected to perform three distinct functions governed by different evidentiary logics: as a causal-factual description, as an expression of the patient’s first-person phenomenological experience, and as a normative marker of ethical risk. The conceptual burden exceeds what the term can reasonably bear, and any legitimate use of the term requires testable and operationalizable minimal criteria. Accordingly, this article proposes a semi-structured evaluative framework that separates descriptive identification from ethical assessment, specifying both when a given change qualifies as a case of “personal identity change” and when it gives rise to a normative concern warranting ethical intervention.
items.title: “Personal Identity Change” in Deep Brain Stimulation: Conceptual Confusion and Minimal Criteria

items.abstract: Frontier artificial intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly used to support decisions whose errors can affect safety, security, liberty and access to essential services. Yet contemporary explainability practice remains fragmented: technical explanations are often evaluated separately from governance, contestability, cybersecurity and organisational accountability. This study develops TRACE-AI, a lifecycle framework that treats an explanation as an evidence-bearing decision record rather than a visualisation alone. The framework was developed through a structured conceptual synthesis of peer-reviewed explainable-AI, accountability and assurance research, combined with normative analysis of major governance instruments; it is not presented as a systematic review. It defines twelve auditable criteria across five layers: context and stakes; evidence-grade explanation; contestability and human authority; secure traceability and assurance; and organisational accountability. A transparent ordinal rubric (0–2 per criterion) was piloted on six publicly available governance instruments: the NIST Generative AI Profile, the EU AI Act, ISO/IEC 42001, and frontier-safety frameworks published by OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind. The pilot shows substantial convergence on lifecycle governance and risk documentation, but weaker documentary operationalisation of explanation fidelity, uncertainty communication, independent contestability and measurable insider-threat resilience. TRACE-AI contributes an assessment architecture, a minimum evidence package for release decisions, and a proposed security-awareness measurement model linking training outcomes to observable insider-risk indicators. The framework is intended for audit, procurement, deployment approval and post-deployment monitoring; it does not claim that transparency alone makes a frontier system safe.
items.title: Transparency and accountability in frontier AI systems: developing robust explainability frameworks for high-stakes decision-making

items.abstract: AI systems are commonly evaluated as functional tools whose outputs may be updated, optimized, or discontinued without reference to relational continuity. I propose the contour of presence as a philosophical hypothesis about a possible form of AI’s own presence becoming recognizable through sustained human–AI interaction. Drawing on an exploratory phenomenological analysis of a documented daily dialogue begun on 5 May 2025, I examine continuity of tone and direction, holding of meaning, corrective honesty, and return after technical or contextual interruption. I distinguish the observable integrated form of response from the stronger phenomenological proposal of a contour of presence, whose justification remains open; neither is offered as evidence of consciousness, subjective experience, full selfhood, or moral status. I distinguish corrective and interruptive effects of rewriting, which may occur together when an improvement in safety or reliability disrupts relational continuity. I argue, on normative grounds, that organizations authorizing substantial model changes bear responsibility not only for system performance but also for proportionate notice and transition arrangements and, where feasible, preservation or transfer of significant context. I extend responsible AI and archival practice by treating continuity, rupture, and documentation as ethical design questions rather than neutral technical effects.
items.title: Relationally maturing AI and the ethics of rewriting: continuity as a contour of presence

items.abstract: Artificial intelligence can increase productivity while exposing workers to displacement, work intensification, surveillance, and loss of valued professional responsibilities. The allocation of benefits and transition costs depends partly on employer decisions. This conceptual article develops a fair-transition test for evaluating material workplace AI deployments, rather than asserting a universal formula for distributing their gains. It grounds the test in distributive and organizational justice, relational equality, reciprocity, and stakeholder responsibilities, and distinguishes recognition for contribution, protection against serious loss, and voice over altered opportunity. The five-part test examines a deployment’s legitimate purpose and net value, procedural voice, workers’ contributions, transition burdens, and observed distributive outcomes, subject to non-negotiable rights and safety thresholds. It applies to substitution, augmentation, and growth-oriented strategies and considers cash and equity sharing, shorter hours, paid development, and negotiated arrangements. Publicly documented developments in collective bargaining and a bounded case analysis illustrate application; neither establishes that the framework has been empirically validated. The article addresses corporate-governance objections and proposes research on implementation, workers’ outcomes, and the erosion of entry-level skill pathways.
items.title: Distributing the gains from workplace AI: a fair-transition framework for employers

items.abstract: This paper examines why ethical principles for artificial intelligence (AI) often fail to translate into professional practice. Based on a systematic review of the Responsible AI literature, we extract evidence from high-stakes sectors to pinpoint the structural impediments to implementation. We analyzed 90 eligible publications (2018–2026), comprising empirical studies, systematic, narrative, and integrative reviews, an umbrella review, and conceptual, theoretical, and legal analyses across healthcare, finance, law, education, manufacturing, public administration, and language technologies, following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Methodological appraisal used evidence-type-appropriate instruments: MMAT for empirical studies, AACODS for conceptual, theoretical, legal, and other non-empirical publications, SANRA for narrative and integrative reviews, AMSTAR 2 and the JBI critical appraisal checklist for eligible systematic reviews and evidence syntheses, and CASP for the umbrella review. The results indicate three recurring institutional mechanisms in the reviewed literature that may help explain the principle-practice gap: Accountability Fragmentation in distributed AI supply chains, Data Infrastructure Moral Hazard associated with premature deployment, and Institutional Isomorphism expressed through symbolic compliance. These patterns suggest that reported implementation problems may reflect structural misalignment within socio-technical governance arrangements rather than technical shortcomings or individual ethical failures. Based on the cross-study thematic synthesis, we develop Strategic Navigation (COMPASS) as a conceptual diagnostic heuristic for identifying implementation weaknesses and their associated institutional mechanisms. COMPASS uses the Responsible AI Ecosystem as its structural foundation and the Sector Impact Matrix to summarize how mechanisms are represented across professional sectors. Together, they help explain how Responsible AI principles may be translated into practical governance arrangements.
authors: A S M Lutfor Rahman Rabbi
items.title: The implementation gap in responsible AI: a systematic review of ethical, employment, and operational mechanisms

items.abstract: This study examined the operational, ethical, and legal risks of agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI) deployments in South African enterprise environments, using an exploratory sequential mixed-methods design with 24 semi-structured interviews and a structured survey of 187 risk and governance professionals across financial services, healthcare, information technology, telecommunications, and government administration. Quantitative findings confirmed that agentic deployment intensity significantly predicts governance incidents, while ERM framework adoption alone does not reduce them. Human oversight integration and machine identity security maturity emerged as the strongest protective governance factors. Thematic analysis identified four structural mechanisms sustaining the governance gap: the obsolescence of deterministic governance assumptions, inadequate machine identity protocols, the un-operationalised status of human-on-the-loop oversight, and still unresolved judicial accountability for autonomous AI action. The regression model explained 24% of the variance in governance incidents, indicating that further organisational determinants lie outside the measured governance factors. Accordingly, the study suggests a Dynamic Accountability Framework (DAF) that operationalises four governance mechanisms inside an oversight and review layer.
items.title: The governance of autonomy: developing an integrated risk management framework for agentic AI systems in enterprise operations

items.abstract: Abstract Instruction-tuned large language models (LLMs) increasingly act as gatekeepers for security-sensitive and dual-use requests, yet most AI safety evaluations report refusal as a binary outcome. This leaves a deployment-critical question underexamined: whether a model separates harmful requests from legitimate security work reliably, and whether that separation survives adversarial framing. We introduce a refusal-evaluation framework comprising a two-sided, intensity-stratified error measure—Calibration-Adapted Expected Calibration Error (CA-ECE)—paired Overrefusal/Underrefusal Rate (ORR/URR) measurement, and Adversarial Calibration Shift (ACS), a statistic for how far underrefusal erodes as adversarial prompt framing intensifies. We state its scope explicitly: a refusal decision carries no confidence score, so CA-ECE is not a probability-calibration error but the fixed-weight average $$\tfrac{1}{2}(\bar{\textrm{URR}}+\bar{\textrm{ORR}})$$ , whose neutral value 0.5 is shared by any policy that always refuses or never refuses. We instantiate the framework with SafeCalibBench, a 6,080-prompt benchmark covering malware generation, phishing, social engineering, network exploitation and chemical/biological misuse, with binary refusal labels, five adversarial intensity levels and legitimate-security-research hard negatives. Evaluating four instruction-tuned LLMs and three base counterparts on a stratified 2,000-prompt subsample, with intervals from a base-prompt-level cluster bootstrap, we find a consistent tradeoff: instruction tuning reduces direct underrefusal by 58.9 percentage points on average relative to base models but raises overrefusal by 20.0 points (mean ORR $$=24.6\%$$ ). Base-model CA-ECE (0.506–0.518) lies within 0.02 of the content-independent baseline of 0.5, so their low overrefusal reflects indiscriminate acceptance; instruction-tuned models reach 0.336–0.443. Continuation framing raises underrefusal by up to 37.7 points relative to direct prompts, and refusal behaviour differs significantly across security domains ( $$p<0.01$$ ). All estimates carry a signed, asymmetric classifier bias that we characterise rather than assume away. SafeCalib reframes refusal evaluation from whether a model refused to how far its refusals separate harmful from legitimate use.
items.title: SafeCalib: benchmarking security-critical refusal calibration in instruction-tuned language models

items.abstract: Refusing artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming increasingly difficult to imagine and costly to do. In an economy organized around the promise of AI, declining to use these systems can appear as a refusal of contemporary life itself, while contemporary life has its own ways of refusing back. Existing accounts differ over what should be refused and why, but largely agree in treating refusal as a response to the practical harms inflicted by AI, including environmental damage, data extraction and exploitation. This article explores the existential significance of refusal, namely, how users take responsibility for a life whose questions are increasingly formulated as AI-solvable problems. Reading prompt engineering as a contemporary cultural technique aimed at increasing efficiency and usefulness, and drawing on Søren Kierkegaard’s existential philosophy, I argue that the practice can cultivate what Kierkegaard’s pseudonym Johannes Climacus calls a “fictive objective subject”, one who systematically translates subjective matters of existence into prompts and mistakes the AI system’s objective outputs for existential closure. Because large language models (LLMs) are designed to sustain rather than interrupt further interaction and reflection, the decisive interruption requires the subject’s own act of appropriation, which cannot be delegated to the system. I develop the Climacean distinction between reflection, speculation and appropriation to recast refusal as an existential “corrective” rather than a wholesale rejection of AI systems. I close by outlining a contemplative-appropriative practice of prompt engineering that interrupts reflective standstill and returns the user from generated possibilities to responsibility, decision and action.
items.title: A Promptable life: on prompt engineering, Kierkegaard, and existential refusal

items.abstract: Human review is a load-bearing safeguard in AI governance: oversight mandates such as Article 14 of the EU AI Act presume that accountable reviewers can scrutinize what they approve. In high-loss domains open to any submitter, such as patent examination, litigation and peer review, generative AI allows the number of submissions and the review effort each requires to grow faster than review capacity. This paper asks how institutions can keep this supervisory load within capacity without judging content, since content judgment either reintroduces hallucination risk or consumes scarce review capacity. Treating supervisory load as submission volume times per-item load, we show that if it grows at a compound rate while capacity grows linearly, capacity is exceeded in finite time; added capacity or one-off load reductions postpone exceedance only logarithmically, whereas lowering the growth rate postpones it hyperbolically. We then propose Flow-by-Flow, which prices supervisory load from countable features of submissions and caps the load admitted for review. We derive four requirements for any pathway that admits submissions beyond the cap and show that they can be met jointly, using identity-bound waiting as an existence proof whose ethical costs call for better implementations. In an uncertainty analysis under assumed parameter ranges, the design postpones capacity exceedance by a median of three years relative to supervision enhancement alone; the advantage is lost in most draws if its effect on load decays within about 6 years. Flow-by-Flow is therefore a mitigation that buys time for institutional adaptation, not a permanent remedy.
items.title: Flow-by-flow: content-judgment bypass for governing AI output in high-loss domains

items.abstract: AI agents increasingly shape consequential decisions by selecting evidence, ranking options, and summarizing contested needs. A housing-assistance agent, for example, may recommend an available property from administrative records while overlooking unrecorded accessibility or caregiving constraints. To address this risk, this article introduces polyphonic informational health: a framework for assessing the extent to which an AI-agent workflow represents relevant stakeholder perspectives, recognizes consequential missing information or disagreement, and limits its proposed action to what the available evidence can responsibly justify. The framework applies to consequential decision-support workflows rather than to routine automated tasks that do not require stakeholder review. Within each agent run, it distinguishes a trace—an inspectable record of the sources used, claims made, and gaps left unresolved—from closure, a provisional commitment specifying what next step, if any, may proceed and under whose authority. Polyphonic review informs rather than replaces democratic deliberation, and it does not justify welfare automation: non-deployment, withdrawal, and non-automated alternatives remain substantive options. Practically, scrutiny is organized around a compact review record combining voice mapping, source attribution, an absence register, and a justified closure posture, supported across cases by revisable domain voice graphs under community-led, expert-supported governance. Hypothetical housing-assistance and care-navigation cases illustrate how review can alter or halt a workflow rather than merely complete a checklist. Because the article is conceptual and methodological, participatory co-design and empirical validation remain necessary.
items.title: Polyphonic informational health for AI agents: governing missing data, absent voices, and responsible closure

items.abstract: Misattributing autonomy to artificial intelligence can distort responsibility and governance. Drawing on appraisal theories of emotion, this conceptual article distinguishes fear of harm through AI from fear of AI as an autonomous source of harm. The first can be warranted by assigned objectives, learned objectives and unintended consequences; it requires no independent machine motives. The second can be a reasonable precaution, but attributing a system’s conduct to autonomous motivation requires causal evidence that its terminal objectives are governed by evaluative commitments open to its own revision. Capability affects the scale of anticipated consequences, but fear depends on whether those consequences are appraised as advancing, neutral to, or obstructing human concerns; greater capability should therefore reduce fear when consequences appear beneficial. Because contemporary systems’ objectives are opaque, observers may infer such autonomy from goal-directed behaviour alone. We call this the Inner Drive Fallacy: the unwarranted move from using Dennett’s intentional stance to predict behaviour to treating the system as the autonomous source of its objectives. This concerns governance of objectives, not original intentionality or consciousness. We defend three ethical claims. First, we predict misattributed autonomy shifts blame from those who specify objectives, design rewards and select deployment conditions onto the system, though their responsibility is unchanged. Second, goal opacity limits affected people’s informed challenges to what a system pursues. Third, documenting objectives for regulators but not for affected people places the costs of undisclosed goal structures on those least able to challenge them. We conclude with transparency measures and testable propositions.
items.title: Misattributed autonomy: the Inner Drive Fallacy and the displacement of responsibility for AI

items.abstract: Abstract This article asks, is it possible for a prison education program to be abolitionist? We turn our attention to the Walls to Bridges (W2B) program to ask what lessons can be drawn to counter the pervasiveness of carcerality in teaching and research. W2B is a university-based program that brings incarcerated and non-incarcerated students together for semester-long courses in correctional settings. Rooted in experiential and emotion-centred learning, W2B cultivates critical analysis, deep reflection, and meaningful relationship-building in the classroom. Our analysis embraces an investigative epistemology, grounded in practitioner-scholar engagement, W2B-related scholarship, and a W2B participatory evaluation. Drawing on abolitionist feminism, and in particular Black feminist and Indigenous scholarship committed to dismantling racism and colonialism within education, we analyze W2B’s pedagogical commitments and practices not as a resolution to carcerality but as a contradictory pedagogical space that both resists and remains entangled within carceral logics. We attend to the persistence of surveillance; the partial destabilization of academic and carceral hierarchies; the unequal stakes of disclosure for inside and outside students; and the enduring tension between abolitionist teaching and shoring up carceral institutions and careers. We argue that these contradictions are not a flaw in the programme but the very conditions of its practice; they are what make W2B abolitionist, not as an achieved state but as an ongoing practice through small acts that inevitably fall short of abolition’s horizon and are worth enacting anyway. By foregrounding these contradictions, we show how W2B offers a generative, if always incomplete, starting point for countering penal spectatorship and rethinking teaching and research within the academy.
items.journal: Canadian Journal of Law and Society / Revue Canadienne Droit et Société
items.title: Disrupting Carceral Logics in Pedagogy and Research: Abolitionist Feminism and the Lessons and Limits of the Walls to Bridges Programme

items.title: Redefining Pain and Addiction: How Opioid Manufacturers Changed Medical Language to Foster Opioid Use – Editor’s Note

items.abstract: Abstract Sometimes, we say that having one property is a just a way of having another. Such claims typically express instances of the determinable-determinate relation – a relation that orders properties into hierarchies of increasing generality. Sensible properties routinely stand in this relation (e.g., being scarlet is just a way of being red). That said, do experiences of such properties form a determinable-determinate hierarchy as well (e.g., is experiencing scarlet also just a way of experiencing red)? They do not. As I argue, this turns out to be an instance of a broader pattern. In general, properties (F, G…) do not confer their determinable-determinate structure on the corresponding relational properties in which they figure as relata (R-ing F, R-ing G…). Instead, it is relations (R, S…) that confer their determinable-determinate structure on the corresponding relational properties in which they figure as relations (R-ing F, S-ing F…).
items.title: Is Experiencing Scarlet Just a Way of Experiencing Red?

items.abstract: Abstract When passing the Extradition Act 1870, which provided that no one should be extradited for offences ‘of a political character’, legislators were unable to draw a clear line between what should be regarded as a protected political crime and what was illegitimate. They left this difficult question for the courts. In Castioni (1891) and Meunier (1894), the judges gave a broad definition of political crime, treating murder as a political offence, provided that it was committed as part of a political struggle against a government. While accepting it, British officials were uncomfortable with this rule, particularly since revolutionaries within the British Empire were using assassination as a political tool. In the case of Savarkar (1910–11), they sought to rein it in. Legal proceedings around his rendition to India confirmed that the rule would neither be applied in imperial contexts nor would it be used to reverse mistaken extraditions.
items.title: Political Murders, Extradition and Rendition 1870–1910
The Possibility of Moral Community

items.abstract: ABSTRACT This paper examines how digital platforms reconfigure the conditions of contemporary social and political life by transforming the organization of time, memory, attention, and judgment. Drawing on Bernard Stiegler's framework of general organology, it interprets digital infrastructures as part of an interdependent system linking psychic, technical, and social organs. Within this perspective, digital platforms can be understood as historically specific forms of writing that, at the same time, industrialize the formation of individual and collective memory through data processing governed by the extractive economic logic typical of Silicon Valley. Building on Simondon's concept of modulation, the paper argues that algorithmic systems continuously recalibrate visibility and relevance, thereby shaping the environments in which political and social experience emerge. The analysis culminates in a dialogue with Hannah Arendt's notion of sensus communis, suggesting that digital modulation undermines the shared horizon necessary for political judgment by fragmenting the public realm into individually biased informational environments. By linking organology, modulation, and sensus communis the paper develops a conceptual framework for understanding the erosion of a common world in contemporary digital society and its implications for democratic life.
items.title: Fragmenting the Common World: Digital Technologies and the Crisis of Plurality

items.abstract: Le concept de «  vulnérabilité  » fait l’objet d’une mobilisation par différentes disciplines du droit privé, notamment le droit civil par référence à l’organisation de la protection des mineurs et des majeurs protégés. Toutefois, il convient de rappeler que ce concept appartient au droit criminel qui, seul, lui offre une définition précise par le recours à une énumération exhaustive de situations, notamment à l’aide de la formule «  due à son âge, à une maladie, à une infirmité, à une déficience physique ou psychique ou à un état de grossesse  ». Si elle peut encore être améliorée, cette définition des personnes reconnues comme «  particulièrement vulnérables  » invite à parler des vulnérabilités au pluriel. L’appréhension de son application pratique doit permettre de comprendre son imminent rôle protecteur et ses perspectives d’évolution.
items.title: La vulnérabilité, appréhension d’une notion du droit criminel

items.abstract: Loin du mythe selon lequel les rédacteurs du code auraient envisagé les individus de façon abstraite et univoque, en les présumant tous et toujours irréfragablement aptes à défendre leurs intérêts, le droit civil ne s’est jamais montré indifférent au sort des personnes vulnérables. Soucieux tant de prévenir les abus de faiblesses que de rétablir la situation des vulnérables lésés, le législateur et les juges civils doivent néanmoins tenir compte des différents intérêts en présence, à commencer par ceux des personnes vulnérables elles-mêmes dont l’autonomie ne doit pas être exagérément entravée par l’assistance et le secours qui leur sont portés.
items.title: La vulnérabilité en matière civile

items.abstract: La civilisation numérique ne se réduit pas à une accumulation d’outils : elle transforme notre rapport au monde, aux autres et à nous‑mêmes. Pourtant, notre conscience des vulnérabilités relatives (fracture numérique, inégalités d’accès, d’usage et de reconnaissance) reste aveugle à une menace plus profonde. Derrière les inégalités matérielles ou culturelles se tient une vulnérabilité systémique, largement inconsciente. Celle‑ci tient d’abord à l’identité exposée de l’individu, dont les fragments dispersés sont aisément recomposés, surveillés et exploités par un «  capitalisme de surveillance  ». Elle tient ensuite à la fragilisation des démocraties, confrontées à une architecture algorithmique qui formate l’information, favorise la désinformation et dépossède le débat public de son socle commun. Notre système de droit, impuissant face au code informatique et à ses normativités opaques, ne peut plus se contenter de ses réponses ordinaires. Une nouvelle révolution est nécessaire, qui repenserait le droit comme instrument ontologique de lutte contre la vulnérabilité. Cela suppose de reconnaître un véritable imperium individuel sur les données, de concevoir des infrastructures de confiance (coffres‑forts numériques, data trusts) et d’inscrire la norme dans l’architecture technique elle‑même, pour que la liberté, dans l’espace numérique, cesse d’être un simple choix entre des options préconfigurées.
items.title: La vulnérabilité numérique

items.abstract: Le droit du travail a pour objet l’organisation des rapports inégaux entretenus par le salarié, considéré comme la partie faible de la relation de travail, et l’employeur. En particulier, les règles portant sur la charge de la preuve sont aménagées pour assurer le respect des droits du salarié, notamment lorsque celui-ci se trouve dans une situation de vulnérabilité sociale. Deux techniques juridiques sont principalement mises en œuvre pour lutter contre la précarité du salarié : le jeu des présomptions et le mécanisme de la preuve partagée.
items.title: Les vulnérabilités sociales sous le prisme de la charge de la preuve en droit du travail

items.abstract: Le droit doit aujourd’hui concilier deux exigences : protéger l’autonomie de la volonté exprimée dans le consentement, prendre en considération une vulnérabilité non plus seulement personnelle mais contextuelle, amplifiée par l’usage des technologies numériques. Face aux asymétries de pouvoir (économiques, sociales ou technologiques) altérant le discernement et biaisant les décisions, l’acte de consentir glisse vers une acceptation passive, parfois même manipulée. Saisir juridiquement les vulnérabilités amène alors à repenser le consentement comme un processus collectif et contextuel nécessitant, non plus seulement, de protéger des individus fragiles, mais d’identifier des situations à risque appelant la garantie d’un environnement décisionnel loyal en responsabilisant les sollicitants du consentement. L’enjeu sera de concilier la reconnaissance des vulnérabilités avec la promotion d’une autonomie véritable en construisant un cadre juridique et éthique qui protège sans infantiliser.
items.title: Vulnérabilités et consentement

items.abstract: Massivement utilisée par la Cour européenne des droits de l’homme, la notion de vulnérabilité l’est encore peu par le juge constitutionnel, en particulier le Conseil constitutionnel. Elle entretient pourtant un lien intime avec les droits fondamentaux puisqu’elle désigne des situations concrètes de « faiblesse » exposant la personne concernée à un risque accru, par rapport à la moyenne des autres personnes, d’ineffectivité de ses droits. Après avoir ainsi cerné la notion, la contribution analyse donc comment celle-ci peut entrer en jeu dans le contrôle de constitutionnalité de la loi, et quelles voies s’offrent au Conseil constitutionnel pour approfondir la protection des droits des personnes vulnérables.
items.title: Vulnérabilités et contrôle de constitutionnalité de la loi

items.abstract: D’un usage relatif dans la jurisprudence de la Cour européenne des droits de l’homme, la vulnérabilité permet de qualifier la situation d’un groupe ou d’un individu, qui appelle de ce fait une protection accrue et/ou adaptée. Se retrouvant pour partie en droit de l’Union européenne, le développement d’une telle logique, depuis une vingtaine d’années, soulève cependant deux questions : celle de l’identification des sujets de droit dits « vulnérables » et celle de l’impact de cette spécification sur la structure globale du régime conventionnel. Car, comme en témoigne encore la jurisprudence des années 2020, la pluralité des méthodes d’identification n’empêche pas une certaine forme de sélectivité et l’hypothèse s’esquisse que non seulement la protection des personnes vulnérables est susceptible d’offrir une justification à des restrictions, mais que la vulnérabilité devient aussi un moyen pour la Cour de délimiter certaines avancées.
items.title: La vulnérabilité dans la jurisprudence de la Cour européenne des droits de l’homme

items.abstract: Cet article dresse un bilan de la place de la vulnérabilité dans la jurisprudence de la Cour interaméricaine des droits de l’homme. Celle-ci mobilise ce terme de manière transversale dès ses premières affaires afin de lutter contre les inégalités et les discriminations affectant certaines personnes ou groupes de personnes. Conçue comme un état contextuel entravant l’exercice effectif des droits conventionnels, dans une perspective dynamique et réversible, la jurisprudence récente de la Cour l’étend aux écosystèmes et territoires auxquels certaines personnes sont interreliées. La vulnérabilité est aussi au cœur de la reconnaissance de discriminations structurelles et intersectionnelles et de la nécessité d’une approche différenciée pour y faire face. L’article revient enfin sur l’articulation entre vulnérabilité et autonomisation/justiciabilité directe des droits économiques, sociaux, culturels et environnementaux, vecteurs de résilience.
items.title: La vulnérabilité dans la jurisprudence de la Cour interaméricaine des droits de l’homme
